question: The competitiveness of European agriculture depends not only on farmers’ performance, but also on the Union’s ability to ensure stable and affordable access to essential inputs: fertilisers, seed material, plant protection products, precision technology, and equipment.

Recent crises have shown how vulnerable the sector is when external supply chains are disrupted and costs increase sharply at a critical time in the agricultural calendar. In the absence of an industrial strategy aligned with agricultural policy, farmers are expected to achieve European-level performance with tools that are increasingly expensive or hard to find.

This disconnect between production requirements and actual supply capacity weakens the Union’s strategic autonomy and may increase dependence on third markets precisely in sectors that are essential to food security.

Can the Commission indicate whether it is preparing a European strategy focused on critical agricultural inputs that includes stimulation of domestic production, support for industrial capacities in the Member States and rapid response mechanisms for situations where supply is disrupted, in order to protect European farmers from external shocks?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.8.2026) The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) plays a key role in supporting European farmers in the transition towards more resilient and sustainable farming practices. This will also continue in the future programming period 2028-2034.

In addition, the Commission addresses the dependency of agricultural inputs in several ways, such as a proposed dedicated preparedness framework in the amended Common Market Organisation Regulation (EU) 1308/20131, operationalising in the agri-food sector the aims of the Preparedness Union Strategy2 and the EU Stockpiling Strategy3 to ensure continuity of supply during severe crises and emergencies.

In the same context, the Commission has established an Agri-Food Chain Observatory4 with a view to monitoring the developments of costs of inputs such as fertilisers. In 2024, the EU has put forward ambitious measures in the Critical Raw Materials Act5. and to accelerate implementation the Commission adopted the REsourceEU communication6 mobilising a large spectrum of policy tools.

As of 29 May 2026, the Internal Market Emergency and Resilience Act7 applies, helping to enhance the resilience of the internal market and address the vulnerabilities as highlighted by recent crises Furthermore, the recently adopted Fertilisers Action Plan8, aims to strengthen EU’s own production capacity, including by promoting bio-based fertilisers, recycled nutrients and reducing dependency on fossil fuels.

The European Emission Trading Scheme in combination with the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), will steer production, such as fertiliser production, towards decarbonisation, thus helping to shield European farmers from external shocks.
